title: OCD 3 — Test
src: Infection control in dental care settings

mcqs.q: Opportunistic infections mainly affect individuals who are:
mcqs.explain: Opportunistic organisms cause disease in those with weakened immunity; pathogenic organisms cause disease in general.

mcqs.q: Which is a VIRAL infection relevant to dental cross-infection?
mcqs.explain: Hepatitis (and HIV, flu) are viral; TB is bacterial, candidiasis fungal, malaria protozoal.

mcqs.q: Touching contaminated instruments transmits infection by:
mcqs.explain: Direct contact = touching an infected person or object (e.g. contaminated instruments); indirect = touching a contaminated surface.

mcqs.q: Inhaling aerosols generated during dental procedures is which mode of transmission?
mcqs.explain: Airborne transmission = inhaling small infectious particles that remain suspended (aerosols from procedures).

mcqs.q: This diagram shows infection passing between staff and patients. The goal of infection control is to:
opts: Eliminate all microorganisms from the body
mcqs.explain: Infection control aims to break the chain of infection, stopping the agent moving host-to-host and preventing cross-contamination.

mcqs.q: Which organization develops infection-control GUIDELINES for healthcare/dentistry?
mcqs.explain: CDC develops guidelines; OSHA enforces workplace safety standards; OSAP provides education and training.

mcqs.q: OSHA's primary role in infection control is to:
mcqs.explain: OSHA enforces occupational/workplace safety standards, including those related to infectious diseases.

mcqs.q: A bacteriostatic agent:
opts: Inhibits bacterial growth without killing them
mcqs.explain: Bacteriostatic agents (e.g. tetracycline, erythromycin) inhibit multiplication; bactericidal agents (penicillin) kill bacteria.

mcqs.q: Clostridium tetani, which cannot survive in oxygen, is:
mcqs.explain: Anaerobes (e.g. C. tetani) cannot survive in oxygen; aerobes need it; facultative anaerobes grow with or without it.

mcqs.q: Standard precautions are applied to:
opts: All patients regardless of infectious status
Only patients known to have HIV/HBV
mcqs.explain: Standard precautions apply to ALL patients, emphasizing barriers, hand hygiene and safe injection practices.

mcqs.q: Universal precautions (the older approach) focused on protection from:
mcqs.explain: Universal precautions treated all patients as potentially infected with HIV/HBV — protection from blood and body fluids.

mcqs.q: A sharps container and self-sheathing needles are examples of:
mcqs.explain: Engineering controls isolate or remove the hazard (sharps containers, sterile water lines, injury-protection devices).

mcqs.q: One-handed needle recapping and using instruments instead of fingers are:
mcqs.explain: Work-practice controls change the manner of performing a task to reduce exposure.

mcqs.q: For AIRBORNE precautions (e.g. TB), which control is placed FIRST in the hierarchy?
mcqs.explain: For airborne agents like TB, administrative controls (policies, screening) are placed before engineering controls.

mcqs.q: The most common route of pathogen transmission in care is:
mcqs.explain: Hands are the most common vehicle for transmitting pathogens, so hand hygiene is central to infection control.

mcqs.q: This image shows hand-washing at a sink. It is the preferred method when hands are:
mcqs.explain: Alcohol rubs cannot be used on visibly soiled hands — soap-and-water washing is required in that situation.

mcqs.q: Alcohol-based hand rubs are most effective at a concentration of:
mcqs.explain: Alcohol hand rubs (ethanol/isopropanol) act rapidly and are most effective at roughly 60–95%.

mcqs.q: A limitation of alcohol-based hand rubs is that they:
opts: Cannot be used on visibly soiled hands and are flammable
mcqs.explain: They cannot be used when hands are visibly soiled and are flammable, so must be stored away from heat.

mcqs.q: This image shows surgical masks. A mask should be:
opts: Changed for every patient and handled by the side edges
Worn below the nose for comfort
Touched on the front when adjusting
mcqs.explain: Masks are changed for every patient, handled only by the edges, never worn below the nose, and not allowed to touch the mouth.

mcqs.q: A mask worn below the nose or that contacts the mouth is a problem because it:
mcqs.explain: Moisture decreases filtration efficiency; masks must cover the nose and mouth and not contact the lips.

mcqs.q: Protective eyewear should ideally have:
mcqs.explain: Eyewear with front AND solid side shields protects against aerosols, flying debris (amalgam/tooth fragments) and splatter.

mcqs.q: This image shows clinicians in protective attire. When should barriers be removed?
opts: Only at the end of the day
mcqs.explain: PPE protects against spray/spatter and should be removed before leaving treatment areas.

mcqs.q: Regarding gloves, which statement is TRUE?
opts: A new pair is worn for each patient and they are not a substitute for hand-washing
Gloves can be washed and reused
One pair suffices for the whole day
Torn gloves are acceptable if thin
mcqs.explain: Wear a fresh pair per patient, replace torn gloves, never wash/disinfect/reuse, and always wash hands — gloves are not a substitute.

mcqs.q: This image shows a smooth surface being wiped. Such clinical contact surfaces should be:
opts: Barrier-protected or cleaned then disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant
mcqs.explain: Clinical contact surfaces are covered with changeable barriers or cleaned then disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

mcqs.q: Which is a CLINICAL CONTACT surface (not a housekeeping surface)?
mcqs.explain: Clinical contact surfaces include light handles, bracket trays, the chair and door handles; walls, sinks and floors are housekeeping surfaces.

mcqs.q: Housekeeping surfaces (walls, floors, sinks) are best managed by:
opts: Routine cleaning with detergent/water or an EPA detergent-disinfectant
mcqs.explain: Housekeeping surfaces are routinely cleaned with detergent/water or an EPA-registered detergent/disinfectant; fresh solutions are made daily.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is REGULATED medical waste?
mcqs.explain: Regulated waste poses an infection risk: blood/saliva-saturated items, extracted teeth, removed tissues and contaminated sharps.

mcqs.q: This image shows chairside practice. The sharp items should be:
opts: Disposed immediately into a sharps container
Rinsed and left on the tray
mcqs.explain: Contaminated sharps are placed promptly in a puncture-resistant sharps container; regulated waste is autoclaved or incinerated.

mcqs.q: Methods used to TREAT regulated medical waste include:
mcqs.explain: Regulated waste is treated per EPA regulations, commonly by autoclaving or incineration, and stored in color-coded containers.

mcqs.q: In dental radiology, infection control includes:
opts: Wearing gloves and drying films before degloving
Never wearing gloves to keep films clean
Sterilizing the X-ray tube head each time
Reusing contaminated film holders without disinfection
mcqs.explain: Glove up when taking radiographs, heat-sterilize/disinfect semicritical film holders, and dry films with gauze before removing gloves.

saqs.q: List the four modes of disease transmission in the dental setting.
saqs.a: Direct contact (touching an infected person/instrument), indirect contact (contaminated surface/object), droplet (saliva/respiratory droplets) and airborne (suspended aerosols).

saqs.q: Name the three key infection-control organizations and one role of each.
saqs.a: CDC — develops guidelines; OSHA — enforces workplace safety standards; OSAP — education/training and resources for dental asepsis.

Standard precautions apply to ALL patients regardless of status (barriers, hand hygiene, safe injection). Universal precautions = older approach treating all as potentially infected with HIV/HBV (protection from blood/body fluids).

saqs.q: State the three concentration/limitation facts about alcohol-based hand rubs.
saqs.a: Effective at 60–95%; cannot be used on visibly soiled hands; flammable (store away from heat).

saqs.q: List four examples of regulated medical waste.
saqs.a: Blood/saliva-soaked gauze, extracted teeth, surgically removed hard/soft tissues, and contaminated sharps (needles, blades, wires).

saqs.q: Give four rules for the correct use of gloves.
saqs.a: Wear when blood/saliva/mucosa contact is possible; new pair per patient; replace if torn; never wash/disinfect/reuse; gloves are not a substitute for hand-washing.
